overview.body: MASTER unit, and the last lab of the semester. Look at what your game keeps track of during one trip: current_city, total_miles, total_turns, total_hazards, total_escaped, visited_cities, hazards_list, unique_cities, unique_hazards, trivia_asked, and trivia_correct. Eleven variables, all describing the same thing: one player's trip. This lab you bundle them into a Player class. The provided lab-5-2.py is your Lab 5.1 game with those variables replaced by one Player object. It won't run until you write player.py, and when it does, it prints exactly what your Lab 5.1 printed.

mentorQuote.quote: Last week the cities became objects. This week the player does. Same game, same trivia, same beach, and the code finally reads like the story: a player travels to a city, faces a hazard, answers a question.

objectives: Read the provided lab-5-2.py as a spec: every player. call is a method you write
Define a Player class whose constructor starts every trip in San Antonio with twelve private attributes
Write an accessor for every attribute
Write the mutators that change a trip: travel_to, record_hazard, record_trivia, and resume
Give Player a __str__ method and player.py a self-test
Run the finished game: every line matches Lab 5.1
overview.keyConceptsText: An attribute can hold any kind of value, including a list or a set. Player keeps the route in a list (order matters, repeats allowed) and the unique cities in a set (no repeats). A mutator is the only way code outside the class changes a private attribute: the game never touches self.__total_miles; it calls player.travel_to(...), and the method updates five attributes together. The rules for changing the trip live in one place, the class.
overview.textbookReference: Chapter 10: Section 10.2 (Classes) covers class, __init__, self, hiding attributes, and __str__. Section 10.3 (Working with Instances) covers accessor and mutator methods. Your BookEx programs: 10-9 and 10-10 (BankAccount), 10-12 and 10-13 (CellPhone).

An accessor for every attribute, named as the checkpoints list
travel_to(city, miles, turns), record_hazard(name, escaped), record_trivia(correct), and resume(...) update the trip as the checkpoints describe
__str__ returns text like Tester in Houston (200 miles)
The provided lab-5-2.py runs with your player.py and prints exactly what Lab 5.1 printed

content.body: A lab folder with the provided game in it, and the start of player.py: a Player class whose constructor starts a trip in San Antonio, a __str__ method, and a self-test that prints a brand-new player.

The provided lab-5-2.py is your Lab 5.1 game with one change: the variables that tracked a trip are gone, and one Player object holds them. It is also your spec. Every player. call in it names a method you write this lab, and every WAS / NOW comment shows the Lab 5.1 lines that method replaces.

content.quote: Count the variables your game resets at the start of every trip. Eleven, plus the player's name. Every one of them describes the same thing: one player's trip. When a dozen variables always travel together, they want to be one object.

items: Make a lab-5-2 folder. If you set up your folders from the starter zip at the start of the semester, you already have one, with empty copies of player.py, city.py, and function_library.py that the next steps replace.
Copy your Lab 5.1 city.py and function_library.py into the folder, replacing the empty files if there are any. You don't change or submit either one this lab; the game imports them.
Download lab-5-2.py and the four data files from Required Data Files above into the same folder. If your Lab 5.1 city.py doesn't work, download the reference city.py there too and use it instead.
Open lab-5-2.py and read it. Find the line player = Player(player_name) and the WAS / NOW comments around it. Don't run it yet: it needs player.py.

Create player.py in the same folder, replacing any empty file of that name. Start it with a docstring set up like your city.py docstring: player.py first, then the two title lines, Lab 5.2: Deep in the Heart and Deep in the Heart: A Lone Star Journey, then your name, ID, and section lines copied exactly from city.py, and a sentence describing the class.
Two blank lines below the docstring, define class Player: with a docstring that lists its private attributes.

Write __init__(self, name) with a docstring. It creates the twelve private attributes below. Except for the name, each one is named after the Lab 5.1 variable it replaces, with self.__ in front, and each starts the way a new game started in Lab 5.1:
Keep the attributes in this order. Each set comes right after the two lists because it is built from one of them, the same way Lab 4.3 built them.

Below __init__, write __str__(self) with a docstring. It returns the name, the word in, the current city, and the miles in parentheses: Tester in San Antonio (0 miles). On one line the f-string is too long, so put parentheses around the whole returned value and split it into two adjacent f-strings. End the first one with the space after the city, so the second one starts with the ( before the miles. If the space goes missing, you get San Antonio(0 miles).
Below the class, with two blank lines between them, add this self-test at the left edge, not indented, the same pattern as the one in city.py:

content.body: One accessor for each attribute, so the game can read the trip without touching a private attribute.

The trip report, the save file, and the session totals all read the trip. In lab-5-2.py, every one of those reads is an accessor call, like player.get_total_miles(). Twelve accessors in a row is repetitive on purpose: it is the same pattern as City's, and by the fifth one you won't need to look.

items: Below __str__, write twelve accessors, each with a one-line docstring. Each takes only self and returns one attribute: get_name, get_current_city, get_total_miles, get_total_turns, get_total_hazards, get_total_escaped, get_visited_cities, get_hazards_list, get_unique_cities, get_unique_hazards, get_trivia_asked, and get_trivia_correct. Each name is get_ plus the attribute's name without its two leading underscores, so get_total_miles returns self.__total_miles.
Return the lists and sets themselves. The game sorts and counts them where it needs to.
In the self-test, right after print(f' {player}'), add these four lines:

content.body: Three mutators, the methods that change the trip: travel_to, record_hazard, and record_trivia. With them in place, the provided game runs a whole new game from start to finish.

In Lab 5.1, arriving in a city took five lines scattered through the travel loop: miles, turns, the current city, the route list, and the unique-city set. Miss one and the trip report is wrong. Now the game makes one call, and the method keeps all five in step. Nothing outside the class can update four of them and forget the fifth.

content.quote: Read each WAS comment in lab-5-2.py before you write the method that replaces it. The comment lists every variable the old code changed. If your method changes fewer, the trip report will tell me, and it will tell CodeGrade too.

items: Below the accessors, write travel_to(self, city, miles, turns) with a docstring. It records an arrival: set self.__current_city to city, add miles to self.__total_miles and turns to self.__total_turns, append city to self.__visited_cities, and .add() it to self.__unique_cities.

Write record_hazard(self, name, escaped) with a docstring. Add 1 to self.__total_hazards. Then if escaped:, add 1 to self.__total_escaped. Append name to self.__hazards_list and .add() it to self.__unique_hazards.
Write record_trivia(self, correct) with a docstring. Add 1 to self.__trivia_asked. Then if correct:, add 1 to self.__trivia_correct. Write the test that way, not == True, which is a style error.
In the self-test, after the four CP2 lines, add this block:

content.body: One more mutator, resume, so a loaded game can hand its saved trip to a new Player. That finishes the class: every path through the game works, saving and loading included.

Every game starts with a new Player in San Antonio. When the player loads a save, the game still makes a new Player, then calls player.resume(...) with the seven trip values from the save file. Trivia counts aren't saved, so they stay at zero, the same as Lab 4.3.

content.quote: You wrote the same game five different ways this semester, and each time it got better. Module 1 was raw Python. Module 2 added loops and functions. Module 3 added files. Module 4 added dictionaries. Module 5 brings it home with objects. Every rewrite taught you something the last one couldn't, and that is how you learn to build things that last.

items: Below record_trivia, write resume(self, current_city, total_miles, total_turns, total_hazards, total_escaped, visited_cities, hazards_list) with a docstring. The definition line is long, so break it after total_turns, and line the rest up under self.
Set the seven matching attributes from the seven parameters.
Then rebuild both sets from the new lists: self.__unique_cities = set(visited_cities) and self.__unique_hazards = set(hazards_list).

permittedTechniques.notPermitted: Anything outside the toolbox above. One course rule on top of that: to show a number to a set number of decimal places, format it in an f-string, like f'{rate:.1f}', instead of using round(). Here's why: round() changes the number itself, while an f-string changes only what's shown, so the full value is still there for the math that comes later. Picture plotting a course from El Paso to San Antonio: about 500 miles on a steady heading of 108.77 degrees. Round the heading to 109 and you're off by less than a quarter of a degree, which sounds like nothing. Fly it anyway and you miss San Antonio by about 2 miles. Round on every leg of a longer trip and the misses can stack up. Keep the full number for the math, and display only what you print.

ifSomethingBreaks.redirect: The game calls a method you haven't written or named differently. The error names it; compare with the checkpoint that adds it.

ifSomethingBreaks.redirect: Check CP4. resume must rebuild both sets from the lists it receives.
